hints: Look closely at the three fatty acid tails in each triglyceride 1 to 4 and spot which ones contain C=C double bonds.
Remember how a cis C=C double bond puts a kink in the tail, stops molecules packing tightly, and lowers the melting point so the lipid stays liquid.
walkthrough:
**Spot what the molecules are**

All four structures are triglycerides. Each has glycerol on the left joined by three ester bonds to three fatty acid tails on the right.

So the only difference is the fatty acid tails.

**Recall oil versus fat**

Fats are solid at room temperature because they contain mostly saturated fatty acids with straight tails that pack tightly.

Oils are liquid at room temperature because they contain unsaturated fatty acids with C=C double bonds that cause kinks and prevent tight packing.

**Classify 1 to 4**

Molecule 1: three tails of $(CH_2)_{16}CH_3$, no C=C. Fully saturated.

Molecule 3: three tails of $(CH_2)_{14}CH_3$, no C=C. Fully saturated.

Molecule 2: two saturated tails plus one tail with $(CH_2)_7CH=CH(CH_2)_7CH_3$, one C=C. Unsaturated.

Molecule 4: one saturated tail plus two tails with C=C, one has one double bond and one has two double bonds. Highly unsaturated.

**Pick the oil molecules**

Molecules 2 and 4 contain unsaturated fatty acids, so they have lower melting points and are found more in liquid oils.

Molecules 1 and 3 are fully saturated, so they pack well and are found more in solid fats.

options.A: 1 and 3 are both fully saturated with no C=C bonds, so they would pack tightly and be found more in solid fats, not oils.
options.B: Molecule 1 is fully saturated and typical of a solid fat, even though molecule 4 is unsaturated and typical of an oil.
options.C: Molecule 2 is unsaturated and correct for an oil, but molecule 3 is fully saturated and typical of a solid fat.
options.D: Both 2 and 4 contain C=C double bonds that create kinks, lower the melting point, and make them liquid oils.
